actions.name: Review GI/endocrine referral note and biopsy result
actions.result: Referral note from gastroenterology: Dx celiac disease confirmed 3 weeks ago. Duodenal biopsy Marsh 3b (villous atrophy). tTG-IgA 148 U/mL (ref <4). Total IgA normal. Recommended strict gluten-free diet, referral to dietitian for GFD education, repeat celiac serology and micronutrient panel in 3-6 months.

actions.name: Review most recent vitals/weight from chart
actions.result: Height 165 cm, weight 57.2 kg, BMI 21.0 kg/m2 (stable over past 6 months). BP 112/70 mmHg, HR 76 bpm.

actions.name: Review celiac serology (tTG-IgA)
actions.result: tTG-IgA 148 U/mL (ref range <4 U/mL) — markedly elevated, drawn at diagnosis 3 weeks ago. No repeat yet.

actions.name: Review iron studies/ferritin
actions.result: Ferritin 7 ng/mL (ref 15-150 ng/mL) — Low. Consistent with iron deficiency.

actions.name: Review hemoglobin/CBC
actions.result: Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL (ref 12.0-15.5 g/dL) — Low, microcytic indices noted (MCV 76 fL, ref 80-100 fL).

actions.name: Review 3-day food record in chart
actions.result: Food record lists: tabbouleh salad, kibbeh, regular soy sauce (stir-fry), rolled oats, rice, lentils, hummus, grilled chicken, fish, fruit, labneh, almonds, store-bought granola bar (label not checked).

actions.name: Take detailed gluten-free diet history (sources, labels, eating out)
actions.result: Patient reports reading labels mainly for the word 'wheat' but is unsure what else to look for (barley, rye, malt); says she assumed tabbouleh and kibbeh were fine since they are 'basically a salad' with 'just a little' grain; believed oats are naturally gluten-free and never thought to look for a gluten-free certification; thought soy sauce was 'just soybeans' and didn't realize it could contain wheat.

actions.name: Assess kitchen cross-contact practices (shared toaster, cutting boards, utensils)
actions.result: Patient reports household shares one toaster and wooden cutting boards with gluten-containing bread; no dedicated gluten-free prep area; occasionally reuses a strainer used for regular pasta.

actions.name: Assess social/family eating situations and support
actions.result: Patient describes weekly family dinners at mother's home with shared mezze platters and bread-based dishes (pita, tabbouleh); feels pressure not to seem 'difficult' or offend her mother; has not yet discussed diagnosis in detail with family.

actions.name: Assess GI symptom pattern since diagnosis
actions.result: Patient reports bloating and loose stools have improved somewhat but still occur 2-3x/week, more often after family meals or eating out; fatigue persists.

actions.name: Assess readiness/confidence for dietary change (motivational interviewing)
actions.result: Patient rates confidence in sticking to GFD as 6/10; expresses frustration and self-blame ('I thought I was doing everything right'); open to specific label-reading and cross-contact guidance; motivated by pregnancy planning.

actions.name: Screen for pregnancy planning and relevant nutrient needs
actions.result: Patient confirms she and her husband are trying to conceive within the next 6-12 months; not currently taking a prenatal vitamin.

actions.name: Review current medication/supplement list
actions.result: No current supplements. No prescribed iron, vitamin D, or prenatal vitamin. No other medications.

actions.name: Camera inspection of pantry/label items (patient holds up oats and soy sauce containers)
actions.result: Oats container ingredient panel reads only 'whole grain rolled oats' with no 'gluten-free' certification mark anywhere on the label; soy sauce bottle ingredient list reads 'water, wheat, soybeans, salt.'

actions.name: Patient self-report of weight today via home scale
actions.result: 57.0 kg today, consistent with prior stable weight; no unintentional weight loss reported.

actions.name: Screen for other food allergies/intolerances (distractor check)
actions.result: No known food allergies. Reports occasional mild lactose discomfort with large amounts of milk but tolerates yogurt and cheese; not currently restricting dairy.

actions.name: Assess physical activity level (distractor/context)
actions.result: Walks 30 minutes most days and does yoga twice weekly; no recent change in activity.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Inadequate adherence to a strict gluten-free diet due to incomplete knowledge of hidden gluten sources and cross-contact, in a newly diagnosed celiac disease patient with resulting iron deficiency anemia and vitamin D deficiency, planning pregnancy.
differential: Nutrient deficiency from ongoing villous atrophy due to unintentional gluten exposure (most likely, given dietary history)
Non-adherence due to psychosocial/cultural barriers (family meals, fear of being 'difficult') compounding exposure
Co-existing lactose intolerance contributing to residual GI symptoms (minor contributor, not primary driver)
Malabsorption from incompletely healed mucosa independent of diet (would require more time off gluten before attributing symptoms solely to this)
keyFindings: Food record and self-report reveal unlabeled hidden gluten in tabbouleh, kibbeh (bulgur wheat), regular soy sauce (wheat), and non-gluten-free oats
Shared toaster/cutting boards/strainer create cross-contact risk despite 'strict' self-reported adherence
Ferritin 7 ng/mL, Hb 10.9 g/dL (microcytic), vitamin D 16 ng/mL consistent with malabsorption from active celiac disease
Persistent GI symptoms (bloating, loose stools 2-3x/week) despite reported strict GFD, worse after family meals/eating out
Planning pregnancy within 6-12 months with no prenatal vitamin and low ferritin/vitamin D — nutrient repletion is time-sensitive
Patient's self-report of 'completely gluten-free' conflicts with food record and pantry inspection showing multiple hidden gluten sources (mismatch for teaching)
plan: Provide specific, non-judgmental education on hidden gluten sources: bulgur/wheat in tabbouleh and kibbeh, wheat in regular soy sauce, and the need for certified gluten-free oats
Teach label-reading skills (identifying wheat, barley, rye, malt, and 'may contain' cross-contact statements) and point to gluten-free certification marks
Counsel on kitchen cross-contact prevention: dedicated toaster or toaster bags, separate cutting boards/colanders, careful utensil and surface cleaning

Use motivational interviewing to explore culturally appropriate swaps for family meals (e.g., rice-based tabbouleh with quinoa or certified gluten-free bulgur substitute, gluten-free pita) and collaborative problem-solving for discussing needs with her mother without feeling 'difficult'

Recommend she discuss iron and vitamin D repletion (supplementation) and prenatal vitamin initiation with her physician given pregnancy planning; dietitian to reinforce dietary iron/vitamin D sources (lean meats, legumes, fortified gluten-free products, safe sun exposure) alongside medical management — refer back to PCP/GI for supplement dosing and monitoring labs
Schedule follow-up visit in 4-6 weeks to reassess adherence, repeat food record, and check symptom trend; coordinate with GI for repeat tTG-IgA and micronutrient labs in 3-6 months

Document ADIME note capturing assessment, nutrition diagnosis (inadequate adherence to GFD related to lack of knowledge of hidden gluten sources, evidenced by food record and ongoing symptoms/abnormal labs), intervention (education, counseling), monitoring/evaluation plan
redFlags: Low ferritin and hemoglobin with planned pregnancy — needs timely repletion before conception
Low vitamin D with reproductive planning — bone health and fetal considerations
Dietitian should not prescribe iron or vitamin D doses or diagnose anemia severity — refer to prescribing clinician for supplementation and lab monitoring
If GI symptoms worsen or alarm symptoms (weight loss, GI bleeding, severe pain) emerge, refer back to gastroenterology promptly
educationPoints: Many traditional Middle Eastern dishes (tabbouleh, kibbeh) are wheat-based via bulgur and are not safe on a gluten-free diet
Standard soy sauce contains wheat; tamari or certified gluten-free soy sauce are safer alternatives
Plain oats are frequently cross-contaminated during growing/processing; only oats labeled 'gluten-free certified' should be used
Villous healing and nutrient absorption depend on strict avoidance of gluten, including trace cross-contact exposure
Family and cultural meal traditions can be preserved with thoughtful ingredient swaps; disclosure to family can be framed around health needs rather than being 'difficult'
Pregnancy planning raises the stakes for correcting iron and vitamin D deficiencies and achieving mucosal healing before conception

profile.encounterType: Nutrition assessment and counseling (initial dietetics visit)

facts.chart: Patient referred for GFD education 3 weeks after celiac diagnosis; reports ongoing mild GI symptoms despite believing she is fully gluten-free.
facts.says: My doctor sent me here because I was just diagnosed with celiac disease and I need help figuring out this gluten-free thing. I thought I had it handled but I'm still bloated sometimes.

facts.chart: Diagnosed with celiac disease 3 weeks ago after years of bloating, loose stools, and fatigue.
facts.says: It took years of bloating and feeling exhausted before anyone figured out what was wrong. The biopsy finally confirmed celiac three weeks ago.

facts.chart: Residual bloating and loose stools 2-3x/week since starting GFD, more frequent after family meals or eating out.
facts.says: I still get bloated and have loose stools maybe two or three times a week, especially after we eat at my mom's or when we go out.

facts.chart: Patient states she has been 'completely gluten-free' since diagnosis.
facts.says: I've been completely gluten-free since I found out. I cut out all the obvious bread and pasta right away.

facts.chart: Reports eating tabbouleh, kibbeh, oats, soy sauce-based stir-fries, rice, lentils, hummus, labneh, grilled proteins.
facts.says: I eat a lot of the food I grew up with — tabbouleh, kibbeh, labneh — plus oatmeal in the morning and sometimes a stir-fry with soy sauce.

facts.chart: Was unaware bulgur wheat in tabbouleh and kibbeh contains gluten.
facts.says: Wait, tabbouleh has bulgur in it, but I didn't think that counted — it's just a little wheat mixed with parsley, isn't it still basically a salad?

facts.chart: Buys regular rolled oats, assuming oats are naturally gluten-free; does not check for gluten-free certification.
facts.says: I thought oats were just oats — naturally gluten-free, right? I never looked for a special label on the container.

facts.chart: Uses regular soy sauce in cooking, unaware it contains wheat.
facts.says: I use regular soy sauce for stir-fries. I didn't realize soy sauce could have wheat in it — I thought it was just soybeans.

facts.chart: Reads labels for obvious wheat flour but does not consistently check for barley, rye, malt, or cross-contact statements.
facts.says: I check if flour is listed, but I honestly don't always know what else to look for — barley, rye, I'm not sure what counts.

facts.chart: Shares one toaster and wooden cutting boards with gluten-containing bread in household; occasionally reuses pasta strainer.
facts.says: We just have the one toaster at home, and I use the same wooden cutting board my husband uses for his bread. Sometimes I'll use the same strainer for pasta too.

facts.chart: Weekly family dinners at mother's home centered on shared mezze platters and bread dishes.
facts.says: Every week we go to my mom's for dinner, and everything is shared — big platters of tabbouleh, kibbeh, bread. It's how we've always eaten.

facts.chart: Reluctant to tell mother about dietary restrictions; fears being seen as difficult or causing offense.
facts.says: I haven't really explained the whole gluten thing to my mom yet. I don't want her to feel like I'm criticizing her cooking or that I'm being difficult.

facts.chart: Reports frustration and self-blame after learning about dietary mistakes; perfectionist tendencies.
facts.says: I'm honestly kind of upset with myself. I thought I was doing everything right, and finding out I've been getting it wrong this whole time is frustrating.

facts.chart: Patient and husband planning pregnancy within next 6-12 months.
facts.says: My husband and I are hoping to start trying for a baby sometime in the next six months to a year, so I really want to get this right.

facts.chart: Not currently taking any iron, vitamin D, or prenatal supplements.
facts.says: I'm not taking any vitamins or supplements right now, no iron pills or anything like that.

facts.chart: Reports ongoing fatigue despite dietary changes.
facts.says: I still feel pretty tired most days, even though I thought cutting gluten would fix that by now.

facts.chart: Weight has remained stable over the past 6 months; no unintentional weight loss.
facts.says: My weight has pretty much stayed the same, I haven't lost or gained anything noticeable.

facts.chart: No known food allergies; mild lactose discomfort with large milk volumes, tolerates yogurt/cheese well.
facts.says: I don't have any food allergies. Sometimes if I drink a big glass of milk my stomach feels off, but cheese and yogurt are fine.

facts.chart: Walks 30 minutes most days, does yoga twice weekly; no recent change.
facts.says: I try to walk every day, maybe thirty minutes, and I do yoga twice a week. Nothing's really changed there.

facts.chart: Eats out roughly twice weekly, often at Middle Eastern or Mediterranean restaurants; does not routinely ask about shared fryers or seasoning blends.
facts.says: We eat out maybe twice a week, usually Middle Eastern or Mediterranean places. I don't always ask about how things are cooked.

facts.chart: Patient does most of her own cooking at home; husband is supportive but not very involved in meal prep.
facts.says: I do most of the cooking myself. My husband's supportive, but he's not really in the kitchen much.

facts.chart: Rates confidence maintaining GFD as 6 out of 10; motivated but overwhelmed by hidden gluten sources.
facts.says: If you asked me to rate how confident I feel about doing this right, I'd say maybe a six out of ten. There's just more to learn than I thought.

facts.chart: No known family history of celiac disease; mother has type 2 diabetes, father has hypertension.
facts.says: No one else in my family has celiac that I know of. My mom has type 2 diabetes and my dad has high blood pressure.

facts.chart: Drinks wine socially about once weekly, no beer (which would contain gluten) consumption since diagnosis.
facts.says: I'll have a glass of wine maybe once a week. I stopped drinking beer completely after my diagnosis.

facts.chart: Occasionally eats store-bought granola bars without checking labels for gluten-containing ingredients.
facts.says: Sometimes I'll grab a granola bar from the pantry as a snack without really checking the label closely.

facts.chart: Has not yet connected with a celiac support group or dietitian-recommended resources.
facts.says: I haven't looked into any support groups or anything like that yet. I didn't really know where to start.

facts.chart: Hopes to leave visit with a clear, practical list of safe foods and swaps, especially for family meals.
facts.says: I just want a clear idea of what's actually safe to eat, especially for the stuff we eat as a family, so I'm not guessing all the time.

facts.chart: Denies blood in stool, unintentional weight loss, severe abdominal pain, or vomiting.
facts.says: No blood in my stool, no real weight loss, no severe pain or throwing up or anything like that.

facts.chart: Reports regular menstrual cycles; no current contraception as actively trying to conceive soon.
facts.says: My periods are regular. We're not using any birth control right now since we're planning to start trying soon.

facts.chart: Reports moderate fiber intake from fruits/vegetables/legumes and adequate fluid intake, around 6-8 cups water daily.
facts.says: I eat a decent amount of fruit, veggies, and lentils, and I'd say I drink maybe six to eight cups of water a day.

facts.chart: Primarily shops at a regular mainstream grocery store; limited access to a dedicated gluten-free specialty market nearby.
facts.says: I mostly shop at the regular grocery store near us. There isn't really a specialty gluten-free market close by.

facts.chart: Food record submitted to clinic lists bulgur-containing dishes, regular soy sauce, and non-certified oats despite patient believing she is fully gluten-free.
facts.says: I filled out that three-day food log you have — I thought it would show I was doing great since everything on there felt safe to me.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she has been 'completely gluten-free' since diagnosis.
mismatches.recordEvidence: 3-day food record (d5) lists tabbouleh and kibbeh (bulgur wheat), regular soy sauce (wheat-based), and non-certified rolled oats — all common hidden gluten sources.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Sincere self-report of adherence can coexist with unintentional gluten exposure from unrecognized hidden sources; the dietitian must cross-check actual food records/pantry items rather than relying on self-report alone, and address this with empathy rather than blame.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports her weight has stayed the same over the past 6 months with no unintentional weight loss.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Weight flowsheet (d6) confirms stable weight 57.2-57.5 kg over 6 months, consistent with patient's report.
mismatches.teachingPoint: This is a confirmatory check (not a true mismatch) illustrating the importance of verifying patient-reported history against objective flowsheet data; here the record supports the patient's statement, reinforcing that weight stability does not rule out malabsorption when iron and vitamin D are low.

objectives.text: Elicit a detailed, non-judgmental diet history that uncovers hidden sources of gluten (bulgur in tabbouleh/kibbeh, wheat in soy sauce, non-certified oats) despite the patient's sincere belief she is gluten-free.
Identify cross-contact risks in the home kitchen and propose practical, low-cost mitigation strategies.
Use motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's emotional response to diagnosis, confidence level, and cultural/family barriers to strict adherence without judgment.

Interpret relevant labs (ferritin, hemoglobin/MCV, vitamin D, tTG-IgA) in the context of active celiac disease and malabsorption, and correctly identify the need for medical (not dietetic) management of supplementation dosing.
Formulate a culturally sensitive, patient-centered plan including specific food swaps for family meals and a follow-up/monitoring plan, documented using the ADIME format.

Recognize pertinent negatives and distractors (lactose tolerance pattern, physical activity, fiber/fluid intake, GI alarm symptoms) and appropriately deprioritize them relative to the core nutrition diagnosis.

Enjoys reading extensively about health topics and tends to research things thoroughly before appointments.
speechExamples: I read a lot about this before our appointment, but clearly I missed some things.
I just want to make sure I'm actually doing this right, not just think I am.
My mom's cooking is basically how I grew up — I don't want this to feel like I'm rejecting her.
Is there a way to still enjoy tabbouleh without the wheat, or is that just gone for good?
I promise I'm not trying to cut corners, I just didn't know what counted.
concerns: Whether she will ever be able to eat family dishes like tabbouleh and kibbeh again
Whether her low iron and vitamin D will affect her ability to get pregnant or have a healthy pregnancy
How to tell her mother about the diagnosis without seeming critical of her cooking or causing tension
Whether she has been inadvertently damaging her gut further despite trying to do the right thing

She was diagnosed with celiac disease 3 weeks ago by her gastroenterologist and was referred to you for nutrition education and support. She reports she has been following a gluten-free diet since diagnosis but continues to experience some mild gastrointestinal symptoms. Review her chart and conduct a comprehensive nutrition assessment.

scenario.openingLine: My doctor sent me here because I was just diagnosed with celiac disease and I need help figuring out this gluten-free thing. I thought I had it handled but I'm still bloated sometimes.
tasks: Take a detailed diet history focusing on the presenting concern
Review relevant laboratory results and relate them to nutrition status
Explore any barriers to dietary management using patient-centered, non-judgmental communication
Provide practical, evidence-based nutrition education appropriate to the patient's needs
Develop a follow-up and monitoring plan

profile.summary: A 34-year-old Lebanese-American architect three weeks post celiac diagnosis believes she is strictly gluten-free, but her food record and pantry reveal hidden gluten in bulgur-based dishes, wheat-containing soy sauce, and non-certified oats, alongside iron and vitamin D deficiency and plans for pregnancy. The case teaches dietetics students to reconcile patient self-report with objective diet history, address cultural/family barriers with motivational interviewing, and coordinate nutrient repletion within scope of practice.
